root_cause.text: A lock ordering inversion in the NFC unregister path caused nfc_unregister_device() to hold dev->dev's device_lock while calling rfkill_unregister(), which acquires rfkill_global_mutex, conflicting with rfkill_fop_write() taking rfkill_global_mutex first and then reaching nfc_dev_down() that tries to take device_lock on the same nfc_dev.
root_cause.evidence: The CVE/commit explicitly shows the ABBA sequence “rfkill_fop_write() -> rfkill_global_mutex -> nfc_dev_down() -> device_lock(&dev->dev)” versus “nfc_unregister_device() -> device_lock(&dev->dev) -> rfkill_unregister() -> rfkill_global_mutex”, and the patch fixes it by removing rfkill_unregister()/rfkill_destroy() from inside the device_lock critical section and calling them only after device_unlock().

intent_record.intent_summary: Initialize a local rfkill pointer to NULL in nfc_unregister_device() to safely support conditional rfkill handling during device teardown.
intent_record.what: A new local variable declaration, `struct rfkill *rfk = NULL;`, was added at the start of `nfc_unregister_device()` alongside the existing `int rc;` declaration.
intent_record.how: This prepares the function to track an `rfkill` object with a defined initial null state, preventing use of an uninitialized pointer if later logic conditionally assigns or checks it during device unregistration.

intent_record.intent_summary: Move rfkill teardown out of the device lock while clearing dev->rfkill under lock to safely unregister and destroy rfkill during device shutdown.
intent_record.what: The code changes nfc_unregister_device() so that when dev->rfkill is present, it stores the pointer in a local variable rfk and sets dev->rfkill to NULL while still under device_lock(), then moves the rfkill_unregister() and rfkill_destroy() calls to a new conditional block executed after device_unlock().
intent_record.how: This causes the device's rfkill pointer to be cleared while holding the lock but defers the actual rfkill unregistration and destruction until after the device lock is released, preventing those teardown operations from occurring inside the critical section and reducing the risk of lock-related shutdown issues such as deadlock or unsafe callback interactions.

Move rfkill teardown out of the device lock while clearing dev->rfkill under lock to safely unregister and destroy rfkill during device shutdown.

relevance_review.reason: Initializing the local rfkill pointer to NULL is a safety/cleanup change for conditional teardown handling, but it does not address the lock ordering inversion between device_lock and rfkill_global_mutex that caused the deadlock.

The change directly addresses the lock inversion root cause by moving rfkill unregister/destroy out from under device_lock while safely clearing dev->rfkill under lock, preventing the problematic device_lock -> rfkill_global_mutex ordering.

candidates.rationale: This is the direct lock-inversion point: it is called while device_lock(&dev->dev) is held, and rfkill_unregister() acquires rfkill_global_mutex, creating the conflicting order against paths that take rfkill_global_mutex first and then try to take device_lock via nfc_dev_down().
Holding the device lock across the rfkill teardown is what enables the deadlock. This statement begins the problematic critical section that later calls rfkill_unregister().

vuln_statements.explanation: This is the direct vulnerable call in the unregister path. It was executed while the NFC device's device_lock was held, and rfkill_unregister() acquires rfkill_global_mutex, creating the lock ordering inversion against paths that hold rfkill_global_mutex first and then reach nfc_dev_down() and try to take device_lock.

This statement starts the critical section that improperly enclosed rfkill_unregister(dev->rfkill). By holding device_lock across the rfkill teardown, it enabled the deadlock-causing lock ordering inversion described in the root cause.

All NFC devices will now get proper RFKILL support as long as they provide

bic_trace_step.code_snippet:
commit be055b2f89b5842f41363b5655a33dffb51a8294
Author: Samuel Ortiz <sameo@linux.intel.com>
Date:   Thu Apr 11 11:52:20 2013 +0200

    NFC: RFKILL support
    
    All NFC devices will now get proper RFKILL support as long as they provide
    some dev_up and dev_down hooks. Rfkilling an NFC device will bring it down
    while it is left to userspace to bring it back up when being rfkill unblocked.
    This is very similar to what Bluetooth does.
    
    Acked-by: Marcel Holtmann <marcel@holtm
bic_trace_step.reason: The shown function body is sufficient because the vulnerable lock ordering is directly visible in the unregister path. In `nfc_unregister_device()`, the new RFKILL teardown is performed first: `if (dev->rfkill) { rfkill_unregister(dev->rfkill); rfkill_destroy(dev->rfkill); }` and only afterward does the code take the device lock in the later block: `if (dev->ops->check_presence) { device_lock(&dev->dev); dev->shutting_down = true; ... }`. The root cause describes a bug where `nfc_unregister_device()` holds `device_lock` while calling `rfkill_unregister()`. That vulnerable construct is not present here, because `rfkill_unregister()` is called before any `device_lock(&dev->dev)` in this function. The commit also introduces the RFKILL callback `nfc_rfkill_set_block()` which calls `nfc_dev_down(dev)`, matching the other side of the potential inversion, but the unregister path shown already avoids taking `device_lock` around `rfkill_unregister()`. Therefore the vulnerable construct is absent in this snippet, and the function already contains the correct ordering that prevents the described deadlock.

bic_trace_step.reason: The diff is sufficient because it shows the full relevant logic in `nfc_unregister_device()` and the lock placement around the rfkill teardown. In this commit version, `nfc_unregister_device()` explicitly does `device_lock(&dev->dev);` and then, while still holding that lock, executes `rfkill_unregister(dev->rfkill);` followed by `rfkill_destroy(dev->rfkill);`, and only afterward calls `device_unlock(&dev->dev);`. This matches the vulnerable construct from the root cause: holding `dev->dev`'s `device_lock` while calling `rfkill_unregister()`, which can acquire `rfkill_global_mutex`. The commit message and diff address a UAF/data-race by reordering netlink notification and adding locking, but there is no change here to avoid the lock-order inversion in the unregister path. When an adapter is removed, it will unregister itself from hci a
bic_trace_step.code_snippet:
commit f0c9103813b3045bd5b43220b6a78c9908a45d24
Author: Eric Lapuyade <eric.lapuyade@linux.intel.com>
Date:   Mon Nov 26 18:06:27 2012 +0100

    NFC: Fixed nfc core and hci unregistration and cleanup
    
    When an adapter is removed, it will unregister itself from hci and/or
    nfc core. In order to do that safely, work tasks must first be canceled
    and prevented to be scheduled again, before the hci or nfc device can be
    destroyed.
    
    Signed-off-by: Eric Lapuyade <eric.lapuyade
bic_trace_step.reason: The snippet is sufficient because it shows the full body of nfc_unregister_device(), which is the function implicated by the lock-ordering root cause. In this version, nfc_unregister_device() no longer takes device_lock() around device_del(): the old code shown in the diff removed the block `device_lock(&dev->dev); device_del(&dev->dev); device_unlock(&dev->dev);` and replaced it with direct `device_del(&dev->dev);` under `nfc_devlist_mutex`. It also adds shutdown handling before unregister: `device_lock(&dev->dev); dev->shutting_down = true; device_unlock(&dev->dev); del_timer_sync(&dev->check_pres_timer); cancel_work_sync(&dev->check_pres_work);`. Therefore, the specific vulnerable construct described in the root cause—holding `dev->dev`'s device_lock while unregistering and reaching rfkill unregister paths—is absent in this function body, so `has_bug` is false. However, the specific fix for the reported vulnerability is not shown here: there is no `rfkill_unregister()` call, nor any explicit change demonstrating that rfkill unregistration was moved outside the device_lock critical section. This commit is about cleanup/work cancellation and shutdown state, not the lock-order inversion with rfkill_global_mutex. So this function does not already contain the identifiable fix for that root cause, making `is_fixed` false.
